notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0022.stoa024.opp-la: Line 1: 'frugi famulum' is odd for the servant of Luke 19 (normally 'nequam', wicked); translated as printed. The final quotation is Matt. 25:21, not 25:22 as cited. Line 3: the sentence 'For the worst things are always mixed with the best' is not from Luke 12:48; the text may be disordered here. Line 4: 'non labentes hospitium' read as 'non habentes'; 'De post' read as 'ne post'. The clause 'ut si credatur vel videat, episcopus, utrum biberit an non, ignoretur' appears corrupt; rendered by sense as 'if anyone sees the bishop, it may not be known whether he has drunk'. 'Castorinas' taken as garments of beaver fur. Verse references to 1 Tim. 3 are partly misnumbered in the edition (e.g. 'Hospitable' is 3:2). Numerous scanning errors were silently corrected.

Line 5: 'gratiæ pretio' ('for the price of grace') is odd; perhaps corrupt for 'pecuniae pretio'. Line 9: 'quod agero pontifex non dubilat, se dubitanter agere dicat' is obscure, probably corrupt ('agere'); translated tentatively. The Matthew citation is given in the text as 16:25; the verse is 16:26. 'Eum sine causa praedavit' read as 'has plundered him'.

Read 'afere' as 'agere' (do). The text has 'promisi' (I promised), which makes little sense with the Spirit as the one addressed. I have read it as 'promisisti' (you promised). 'perpetus' is unclear: it may be 'perpetua' (agreeing with 'regna', perpetual kingdoms) or 'perpetuus' (the Spirit). I have rendered it as 'forever'.

nodes.text: CHAPTER ONE. — Brothers, if anyone recalls the saying in which the Lord rebuked the thrifty servant for keeping back the money he had received to pay out, saying: You should have given my money [to the bankers], and when I came I would have demanded it back with interest (Luke 19:23), he will no longer be an idle hearer and keep the grace of the divine gift granted to him for his own use alone. Instead he will make it shareable with all, and by paying it out more abundantly he will possess it in safety. In this way he will show the fruit of edification both to himself and to very many, and like a fine tree laden with fruit he will be shown not to occupy the ground fruitlessly while he lives, since it is both adorned in itself with its fruit, and all who take fruit from it are fed. The blessed Apostle also invites us to these same things: Do not seek what is your own, but what is others' (Phil. 2:4). And elsewhere: I do not seek what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, that they may be saved (1 Cor. 10:33). For this reason we, to whom the stewardship of the divine words has been entrusted, and who have taken up the flock of Christ to feed and nourish it, do not believe that we shall escape guilt without enormous danger if we do not live in this manner, or even if we fail to preach. And although the wickedness of this life holds us back from preaching these things, the necessity of the command nevertheless summons us. And woe is me already if I do not preach, if I keep the treasure I received long hidden, buried in the earth, that is, in my heart, and if I hold the lamp of the divine word pressed down under a bushel, and do not set it on a lampstand and display it to the eyes of all; and if I do not unlock the bolts of human ignorance with those keys of the kingdom of heaven which all of us priests received in the blessed apostle Peter. [I preach] so that through this I may deserve to hear, according to the measure of my tongue: Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful in a few things, I will set you over many: enter into the joy of your Lord (Matt. 25:21). Therefore, fearing to be subjected to those rebukes and punishments, struck by fear of penalty and invited by brotherly love, I no longer speak to the subject people, as I have been accustomed continually to do, but I now turn my words to the very preachers of the people. And to my fellow servants, as an obedient servant, that is, a bishop to priests, a prelate to pontiffs, I will not delay to preach boldly the admonitions of salvation. Nor, if out of regard for charity I pay these things out to my fellow priests, will I claim for myself a privilege of knowledge, or confess myself to be of perfect life when I admonish others about the perfect life; rather, when I dare to speak these things to them, I will hear what I say together with them.

CHAPTER II. — Supported now by divine help, I will set out as far as I am able, and aided by the prayers of those to whom our discourse is directed, I will take the road I have longed for, and placed as it were in the lap of my fellow priests, I will address the priests themselves. Hear me, most blessed fathers, and, if you think it fitting, most holy brothers. Hear me, Levitical stock, priestly seed, sanctified offspring, leaders and rulers of the flock of Christ. Hear me as I both entreat you and fear, as I take anxious thought for our common good and wish to show the honour of the episcopate; so that, when we show the privilege of that honour, we may also seek the merits befitting it, and so that we who know the truth in our heart may not be deceived in our work. For it is right that priestly dignity should first be known by us, and then thus kept by us, so that the saying of the psalmist may be turned away from us: Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he has been compared to senseless beasts and has become like them (Ps. 48:13). The honour, then, brothers, and the sublimity of the episcopate can be equalled by no comparisons. If you compare it to the splendour of kings and the diadem of princes, these will be far inferior, as if you compared the metal lead to the gleam of gold; for you see the necks of kings and princes bowed to the knees of priests, and when they have kissed their right hands, they believe themselves fortified by their prayers. What shall I say now of the common multitude? [The episcopate] has not only deserved to be set above it by the Lord, but has also been commanded by the precepts of the Gospel to protect it with a father's right. So indeed the Lord says to blessed Peter: Peter, do you love me? And he: You know, Lord, that I love you (John 21:15–16). And when he had been asked this a third time, and had followed with a threefold answer, the Lord repeated a third time: Feed my sheep. These sheep and this flock the blessed apostle Peter did not receive alone at that time; he also received them together with us, and with him we all received them. Hence, because they are handed over to priests to be ruled, they are rightly said to be subject to their rulers; because by the shining command of the Gospel we see it no less laid down: The disciple is not above the master, nor the servant above his lord; but it is enough for the disciple to be like his master, and for the servant to be like his lord (Luke 6:40).

CHAPTER III. — You should understand, brothers, that we have set all this out first in order to show that nothing in this world is found more excellent than priests, nothing more sublime than bishops; so that, when we show the dignity of the episcopate before the eyes of bishops, we may both fittingly know what we are, and show what we are by profession through action rather than by name; so that the name may agree with the action and the action answer to the name; lest there be an empty name and an enormous crime; lest there be a sublime honour and a disgraceful life; lest there be a godly profession and an unlawful action; lest there be religious dress and irreligious conduct; lest there be a lofty rank and a shameful excess; lest the chair in the Church be held higher while the conscience of the priest is found lower; lest we feign a dove's speech and have a dog's mind; lest we display a sheep's profession and have a wolf's ferocity; and lest the Lord answer us deservedly through the prophet: This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me (Isa. 29:13). Therefore, brothers, as the cloak adorns the senator, as farming the countryman, as arms the barbarian, as skill in navigation the sailor, and as the quality of their work shows each and every craftsman to be its maker: so nothing else marks out a bishop but episcopal work; so that he may be known by good work rather than by profession to be a bishop more by merits than by being so called by name. For just as we have said that nothing is more excellent than a bishop, so nothing is more wretched if a bishop is in danger concerning holy life, if a priest is held in crime, and a pontiff is polluted with the stains of vices. And as it is lighter to fall from level ground, so it is heavier for one who has fallen from a lofty dignity; for a ruin that comes from on high is shattered by a heavier fall. The episcopal honour is indeed splendid before men; but if it suffers ruin, the grief is great. For the higher the episcopal rank is above the others, the heavier the ruin if it slips through negligence. Great loftiness must have great caution; great honour must be surrounded with greater care. From him to whom more is entrusted, more is required, as it is written (Luke 12:48): For the worst things are always mixed with the best; and elsewhere: The mighty will suffer mightier torments (Wis. 6:7); and: For one who knows the law and does not do it, it is a great sin (James 4:17); and: The servant who knows his lord's will, if he does not do it, will be beaten much (Luke 12:47). For God requires one thing from a bishop, another from a priest, another from a deacon, another from a cleric, another from a layman, or from each and every person. And although God examines the works of all men in his judgement, more is nevertheless exacted from him to whom more is committed; for he will pay greater penalties to whom the care of ruling more numerous peoples has been committed.

CHAPTER IV. — And in order to depict for all priests specifically the manner and pattern of the episcopate itself, we must unroll the apostolic rule, which depicts one by one the acts of bishops. Thus the blessed Apostle says to all bishops: It is a faithful saying (1 Tim. 3:1); as if he said: What I am about to speak of, I speak truthfully, lest anyone think I have lied. He added: If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work (ibid.); that is, if you desire to be a bishop, what you long to be is a great thing, but only if you also embrace the good work at the same time. For if you long to be one otherwise, you cannot be a bishop, because there follows: For a bishop must be irreproachable (ibid., 2). He says irreproachable; for if a bishop is reproached, he is shamefully subjected to fault. And indeed fault drags to guilt, guilt to penalty, and penalty leads on to death. See where the episcopal dignity rolls to. And shortly after he says: The husband of one wife (ibid.). If we look only at the surface of the letter, he forbids a twice-married man to be ordained bishop; but if we climb to a higher sense, he forbids a bishop to usurp two churches; and if you search still deeper within, he warns that a bishop should not be found, after [accepting] catholic doctrine, to hold a heretical opinion, but should join to himself only the Christian, orthodox and catholic faith, so that the bishop may be called the husband of only one wife, the catholic Church. Then there follows, and he says: Sober (ibid.), that is, restrained not only in wine but also in vices; so that he may neither indulge in wine more than is fitting, and may always be found sober in mind. And he added what follows, saying: Prudent. Not worldly prudence, of which it is said that it is foolishness with God (1 Cor. 3:19), but spiritual prudence, that is, one that is both circumspect in deed and skilled in word; so that he may be shrewd as a serpent and simple as a dove (Matt. 10:16). And again he adds: Adorned. If we look at this only according to the sense of the letter, we priests will seek nothing but finer dress; for example, we shall seek garments of beaver fur and silk (1 Tim. 3:2), and the man who has put on the finer garment will think himself higher among bishops. But the holy Apostle does not wish to be understood so, because he teaches that a bishop is to be adorned not in flesh but in mind; so that the priest who pleases God is the one who has a soul ordered towards God. And after this he added: Hospitable (1 Tim. 3:2); so that out of regard for humanity he may receive into lodging those who have no lodging, and bring the needy man without a roof into his house, and not devour alone the gifts of Christ which the goodness of Christ has bestowed on him; and because God loves a cheerful giver, let him give to Christ's poor without grumbling. Then there follows, and he says: Apt to teach (ibid.), that is, let a bishop be so strong in wisdom that he not only teaches sufficiently the people entrusted to him, but can also repel from the catholic Church the contradictions of all heresies; lest through his ignorance he fail to teach the ignorant, and, overtaken by such a mishap, what is written befall him: When the blind leads the blind, both fall into the pit (Matt. 15:14). But whoever knows that he is not such as we have said, let him not seek the priesthood, nor presume to usurp the place of another, especially of one who by the brightness of his wisdom can illuminate the hearts of peoples. He added, and says: Not given to wine (1 Tim. 3:3), that is, not devoted to much wine; so that if anyone [sees] the bishop, it may not be known whether he has drunk or not; lest after a large draught of wine he take delight in the allurement of women, and lest through wine, as the Apostle says, every kind of debauchery be nourished (Eph. 5:18). Next there follows, saying: Not a striker, but modest (1 Tim. 3:3), that is, let him not have wicked hands ready for slaughter, nor strike the consciences of others with depraved suspicions; lest, being found petulant and ready for slaughter, he be judged a prize-fighter rather than a bishop. But on the contrary let him rather bear patiently the injuries inflicted by others, so that he may show to all men the calm modesty of his mind and display firm patience to all. Again he added, saying: Not quarrelsome (ibid.), that is, let the bishop not loose his tongue to abuse, lest with the same tongue with which he offers praises to God and pours out the divine sacrifices he bring forth the poisons of quarrels; for it is not fitting that blessing and cursing should come out together from a bishop's mouth, nor that a man should be cursed by the same tongue by which God is praised; for one spring cannot produce sweet and bitter water. Thereafter he followed, saying: Not covetous (ibid.), that is, not covetous of shameful gain; lest the bishop be held liable through covetousness of gain and nourish avarice, which is the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6:10). Let him, content only with the stipends of his church, not strive at all for what he knows to be superfluous, but rather share willingly with Christ's poor out of the very poverty of his church, as it is written: God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7); and elsewhere: He has scattered, he has given to the poor, his righteousness remains for ever and ever; his horn will be exalted in glory (Ps. 111:9). And he joined on what follows, saying: One who knows how to rule his own house well, having his children in subjection with all chastity (1 Tim. 3:4). He can rule his house well who has kept the chastity of his body. House, he says, that is, let him govern his body with commanding right, lest he himself be subjected to his body, and, given over to the desire of lust, be plunged headlong; but rather let him teach his children the rule of modesty by the example of chastity. For if anyone does not know how to rule his own house, how will he apply diligence to the Church of God (ibid., 5)? This is what we said above: he who cannot cultivate the house of his own heart, how will he apply diligence to many? And he who cannot pull the beam of sin out of his own eye, how will he be able to remove the speck from another's eye (Luke 6:41)? He likewise follows, and says: Not a neophyte (1 Tim. 3:6), that is, one who has recently come to the faith from paganism, or indeed has been joined to the office of the clergy from secular military service. Let such men, then, not so indiscriminately seize the priestly rank, lest, lifted up into pride, they fall into judgement and into the snare of the devil; for what they have not learned over a long time they cannot keep in a short time. And concluding the rule and pattern of the episcopate, he added at the end, saying: But he must also have a good testimony from those who are outside (1 Tim. 3:7), that is, from heretics and schismatics, who outside the holy catholic Church set [leaders] over their profane conventicles; yet the Apostle says that the bishop ought to have these as witnesses and a good testimony about his spotless life and the holy conduct of the bishop; lest perhaps enemies find occasion to disparage the bishop and begin to defame catholic doctrine.

CHAPTER V. — These things having been thus set out beforehand, in this work, as I think, we have felt ourselves freed as if from a great debt, since we have set against the bishops not our own testimonies but those of the holy Apostle, lest they mock our work as if it were common tales. But since the authority of the holy apostle Paul has smiled on us in each point, let them, if they dare, rebuke the Apostle himself rather than us. And although the length of this little book now constrains us, and time urges us to come to the end of this work, yet the concern of brotherly love holds us back, especially for those priests who, dulled by torpor of mind, defame the priestly honour; and who are lamented for having monstrously brought forth a new rule in this age, and, following the example of Gehazi and of Simon, have bought up the grace of the holy episcopate with money, in no way fearing that, since they have bought the priestly honour with money, they have been condemned with Simon by the blessed apostle Peter, as he says: Your money, he says, perish with you, because you thought to buy the gift of the Holy Spirit with money (Acts 8:20). And let those who think they can acquire the priestly rank with money believe that they have received leprosy with Gehazi from holy Elisha (4 Kings 5:27). When we have said these things to them, it ought to have been enough for them to possess their leprosy by purchasing [it]. For just as, when the head is corrupted by more severe diseases, the rest of the body must be lethally drenched by the flood of the disease above; so also those who seem to be the head of the Church corrupt the brotherly body with a pestilent disease, so that nothing in the frame of the whole body can escape unwounded, since the deadly poison of the viciousness of negligent priests has infected it; so that you see everywhere in the Church those whom not merits but money have advanced to the order of the episcopate: a frivolous and ignorant people, who have taken such a man to themselves as priest. If you wish to ask them faithfully who set them over [others] as priests, they answer at once and say: I was recently ordained bishop by the archbishop, and I gave him a hundred solidi so that I might obtain the episcopal grace; if I had not given them, I would not be a bishop today; hence it is better for me to bring gold out of my purse than to lose so great a priesthood. I gave gold, and I bought the episcopate; yet I do not doubt that, if I live, I shall get those solidi back at once. I ordain priests, I consecrate deacons, and I receive gold; for I am confident that I shall no less drive a trade for money from the other orders as well. See, the gold I gave I have taken back into my purse: so I received the episcopate for free.

This, surely, is what grieves me: that the archbishop made a bishop carnally. For on account of money he ordained one spiritually leprous. Your money, he says, perish with you, because you have bought the gift of the Holy Spirit for the price of grace (Acts 8:20–21), and have carried out a miserable trade to the exile of souls. And ignorant and unlearned men at their ordinations cry out and say: You are worthy, and you are just; and wretched conscience says: You are unworthy, and you are unjust. For a bishop of this kind proclaims to the people, saying: Peace be with you. To fleshly eyes indeed he seems like a great bishop, and to the divine gaze he is seen as a great leper. Through money he acquired an order not owed to him, and before God he lost the inner man. The flesh took up the dignity, and the soul lost its honour. The flesh, the handmaid, has become mistress of the soul, and the soul, which was mistress, has become the servant of the flesh. The flesh rules over peoples, and the soul serves a demon. He bought the priesthood for the flesh, and prepared loss for the soul. And what does it profit such a man if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a man give for your soul (Matt. 16:26)? What he gave when he was ordained bishop was gold, and what he lost was his soul. When he ordained another, what he received was money, and what he gave was leprosy. These are the merchandise of the wicked, to their own destruction.

Yet I question our brother and fellow bishop, since I too am a bishop, and I am speaking with a bishop. Tell me, then, for a moment, brother bishop: when you gave money, what did you receive? I received episcopal grace. So I ask you: why is this grace called by such a name? He answers: Why, you ask? As I think, because it is given gratis, therefore it is called grace. So if grace is given gratis, and is not valued in gold, why is grace bought by you with money? He answers: It would not, he says, have been given to me if it had not been bought with money; nor would I have been ordained bishop if I had not given money. Therefore, as appears from your answers, you did not receive grace when you were ordained, because you did not obtain it freely. And so, brother, if you did not receive grace, how could you be made a bishop? For the Lord also says to his disciples: You have received freely, give freely (Matt. 10:8). Why then did you think you could possess free grace for a price? For, as I see, by giving gold you lost [it], and you did not acquire holy grace.

Yet adding once more, I question the brother bishop, lest we seem to have passed over any of the truthful proofs. Who gives episcopal grace, brother? God, or man? You answer without doubt: God. But yet God gives through man: man lays on hands, God bestows grace; the priest lays on his suppliant right hand, and God blesses with his mighty right hand; the bishop initiates the order, and God grants the dignity. O justice, O equity! If money is given to the man, who does nothing more in the ordination than only the service entrusted to him, why is everything denied to God, who bestows the order itself on you? Does it seem just to you that the servant should be honoured and the lord suffer injury; and that the priest should unjustly receive money, and God suffer injury from man? But since God expects nothing from you for the order granted, why does the priest shamelessly expect money from you? God wished to grant [it] to man freely, and the rapacious bishop seeks money from the man for nothing; God, being certainly kind, gave to man freely, and the malignant priest has plundered him without cause! For what do you have that you have not received? And if you have received [it], why do you boast as if you had not received [it] (1 Cor. 4:7)?

CHAPTER VI. — See to what evils the divine order is rolled; see into what disgraces the priests have fallen, who were found worthy to hear from the judge of the world: You are the light of the world (Matt. 5:14). See to whom the nations are subjected, to whom it was said by the Lord: You are the salt of the earth (ibid. 13). So if the bishop is the light of the Church, and is ordained by the Lord so that by the shining eloquence of his preaching he may illuminate the darkness of ignorance and the hiding places of consciences, why is he himself held bound by palpable darkness? And not only does he himself, while he acts wickedly, deservedly perish; moreover he also undeservedly destroys others with him. For if you were found worthy to possess the savour of salt, so that you could season the fields of the foolish, why, made insipid by such a vice, have you offered yourself to be trampled by the unclean feet of swine, so that you can season neither others nor yourself? You also willingly sought the office of the eyes in the body, that is, in the Church, so that the rest of the body might have through you the guidance of light; and now, darkened by a kind of bleariness and fog of vices, you neither present yourself fit for the light, and you take light away from others. Of these eyes it is said in the Gospel: If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light (Matt. 6:22); that is, if the bishop, who deserved to preside in the body as a light, is adorned with holy simplicity and innocence, the whole Church is irradiated with the splendour of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark; that is, if the bishop, who seemed to give light to the body subject to him, is clouded by the blindness of wickedness, what will the other members do, from which the light of the eyes has been taken away? That is, what will the lay multitude do, when the bishop by illicit pleasures and forbidden actions has provoked the multitude of the people to a like abyss of crimes, so that nothing any longer seems unlawful to anyone which is perpetrated by the bishop as if lawful? Rather, men believe that whatever the bishop has found delightful is itself the more praiseworthy; and let no one say that what the pontiff does not hesitate to do, he himself does with hesitation; for you are called bishop by all without hesitation, especially since you are reckoned by that very name: if only the action agrees with the name, and the name joins itself to the action. For what else does 'bishop' mean but overseer, especially since he sits on a raised throne in the Church, and so looks upon all that the eyes of all look upon him? Since, therefore, this is so, why do you show yourself to the eyes of all like a foul mirror, so that they cannot adorn themselves more neatly by your obscurity?

CHAPTER VII. — It is enough for now to have extended our discourse this far, a little, to our fellow priests, in which we have shown both their excellence and their fall, so that, trusting in the loftiness of their honours, they should not fail to seek perfection of conduct, and believe that they may glory in the mere name of priest more than in the work. And although I know that because of this little book many priests who do not wish to do the things we speak of will faithlessly disparage me, I believe nevertheless that very many who do these things, or strive to do them, will faithfully pray for us. But just as we are not weighed down by the attacks of detractors, so we are helped by the prayers of tried and holy men. Come now, sanctifying Spirit, who have helped us in this work with divine inspirations: help all priests, and grant that they may do what you yourself inspired [me] to speak in this little work, so that you may grant to them, together with me, the kingdoms of heaven, which you promised to give to the saints at the end of the ages, forever. Amen.
